Plant Notes: According to Sagun et al. (2010), Acalypha wilkesiana is not most closely related to A. amentacea and is better treated as a species known only from cultivation that is more closely related to A. hispida.
Agdestis perhaps belongs in its own family or in Sarcobataceae (APG IV 2017).
The leaf blades have yellow punctate glands abaxially, and are apparently rarely ever eglandular, while the peduncles and phyllaries are without stipitate glands (Johnson 1971).
The peduncles and phyllaries are usually stipitate-glandular, although occasionally are glabrous (Johnson 1971). The leaf blades do not have the conspicuous yellow punctate glands like A. conyzoides.
The specific epithet was originally spelled as "paronichyoides" in the protologue and on the labels of the type specimens (Pedersen 1967). This epithet has often been changed to "paronychioides".
Gonzalez (1990) considered the description of A. littoralis more similar to A. odoratissima, and that neither were synonyms of A. elegans.

Asparagus densiflorus generally has stems erect to weakly decumbent to 60 cm long, the branchlets typically 3.5 cm or shorter, the cladodes (leaf-like structure) 5-15 mm long, and the berries ca. 5 mm wide with one seed; it was previously misapplied to A. aethiopicus in Florida. Asparagus aethiopicus generally has stems climbing to erect to 1-7 m long, the branchlets typically 4 cm or longer, the cladodes (5)10-40 mm long, and the berries 5-7 mm wide with 1-3 seeds (Jessop 1966; Judd 2001).
Bothriochloa is not monophyletic (Sumadijaya 2015; Welker et al. 2020), and perhaps it, Capillipedium, and Euclasta could be merged with the older name Dichanthium.

Recent taxonomy suggests B. odorata is the species naturalized in Florida, which has some petioles usually with distinct prickles, globose fruits, small midrib bundles completely encircling the fibrous cylinder, and does not have raphide-containing idioblasts in the foliar margin, unlike B. capitata (Noblick 2011, 2014; Sant’Anna-Santos et. al 2015).

The genus Cannabis is here treated as containing one extant polymorphic species (Small & Cronquist 1976; Small 2015). Cannabis is part of the FDA Schedule I. This plant and its prenylated polyketides, THC and cannabidiol, are a subject of interest for their effects on some forms of epilepsy, Tourette syndrome, and other conditions.
In Florida, Casuarina glauca commonly hybridizes with C. equisetifolia (Gaskin et al. 2009).
In Florida, Casuarina glauca commonly hybridizes with C. equisetifolia and rarely with C. cunninghamiana (Gaskin et al. 2009).
The very similar C. richardii is sometimes recognized but only distinguishable by its 16-spored sporangia (vs. 32 in C. thalictroides). However, C. richardii apparently is not found in Florida.

This species is now placed in Coleus, following the taxonomy of Paton et al. (2019) that recognizes Plectranthus as distinct from Coleus. While this species was recognized as P. parviflorus in Plectranthus, the earliest available name in Coleus is C. australis.

This species is now placed in Coleus, following the taxonomy of Paton et al. (2019) that recognizes Plectranthus as distinct from Coleus. Prior taxonomies had differed (Pollard & Paton 2001; Paton et al 2004; Zhong et al. 2010).
Verloove (2014) treated this taxon as a subspecies as C. alternifolius subsp. flabelliformis.

The correct name for this species appears to be Cyperus neochinensis (=Lipocarpha squarrosa). Cyperus aristulatus and C. leptocarpus (=Lipocarpha microcephala) were then both misapplied to this species in Florida (Goetghebeur & Van den Borre 1989; FNA, vol. 23).
Here considered non-native, Webster & Cardina (2004) found the earliest specimen in Florida in Leon Co. from 1843; it was collected in Miami in 1878 (Garber s.n., BRU).
Digitaria subcalva has been considered endemic to Hernando, Hillsborough, Polk, and St. John Cos. and distinct from D. texana (Weakley et al. 2018; Hall 2019).
Macfadyena is considered a synonym of Dolichandra (Fonseca & Lohmann et al. 2015; Fonseca et al. 2017).
The current taxonomy of Egeria recognizes three species which are difficult to identify (St. John 1961; Cook & Urmi-König 1984; Koehler & Bove 2001).
Because of problems with the application of the name E. amabilis, it has been proposed for rejection, in which case E. tenella would become the preferred name for this species (Peterson et al. 2018).
For a revision of the genus see Buitenhuis & Veldkamp (2001).

The merger of Eriobotrya and Rhaphiolepis is supported by recent DNA analyses, which would cause this species to adopt the name Rhaphiolepis bibas. It has also been proposed to conserve the name Eriobotrya, due to its wide use for the loquat, against Rhaphiolepis.
Formerly included in the genus Chamaesyce, this species is reclassified under Euphorbia subg. Chamaesyce sect. Anisophyllum subsect. Hypericifoliae.
Low shrubby forms often used as a hedge and called 'Green Island' may be referred to as F. microcarpa var. fuyuensis (Liao 1996).

Fumaria species are rather difficult to identify (Lidén 1986), and traditionally, F. officinalis has been considered a common species in Florida (FNA vol. 3). However, from three specimens annotated at GH, Lidén did not annotate these as F. officinalis but rather identified the following three species in Florida: F. densiflora (Godfrey 52920, Leon Co.), F. muralis (Genelle & Fleming 31, Pasco Co.), and F. vaillantii (Baltzell 3614, Orange Co.).

In the USA, Gaillardia pulchella is found predominantly from Lousiana west to Arizona and Kansas south to Texas. It is widely cultivated in Florida. It is not native to Florida nor the rest of the eastern USA (Weakley 2020). Small (1929: 16) noted its naturalization in the Halifax River region. A DNA phylogeny found G. pulchella closely related to other species of the southwestern USA (Marlowe & Hufford 2007).

Common Name: SOUTH AMERICAN MOCK VERVAIN; MOSS VERBENA

Plant Notes: Schefflera s.lat. has been shown to be polyphyletic (Plunkett et al. 2005), and this species is placed in the genus Heptapleurum (Frodin et al. 2010; Li & Wen 2014; Lowry & Plunkett 2020).
Based on DNA analyses, this species may move to the genus Themeda (Arthan et al. 2021).
Historically, this species seemed to be found in more tropical parts of Florida. Some of the county occurrences of this species may be I. leucantha.

Lagerstroemia fauriei is allegedly hybridized with L. indica to create some cultivars. However, the name L. fauriei was considered possibly synonymous with L. glabra, a species with 12 or more calyx ridges, unlike L. indica with six superficial, slightly developed calyx ridges evanescent on the calyx tube (Furtado & Srisuko 1969).
The current application of this name was discussed by Wiersema (2014).

This species has been divided into two entities, L. grandiflora s.str. (hexaploid) and L. hexapetala (decaploid). They are morphologically difficult to separate (Nesom & Kartesz 2000) and octoploid hybrids between the two have been reported (Zardini et al. 1991). When two entities are recognized, the application of the name L. grandiflora to plants having mostly lanceolate leaf blades appears to conflict with the type specimens of L. grandiflora that have spatulate and oblanceolate leaf blades. Spatulate and oblanceolate leaf blades were considered to be representative of L. hexapetala (Zardini et al. 1991; Nesom & Kartesz 2000). Although Michaux (1803, vol. 1: 267) represents an early observation for L. grandiflora in Georgia, it is probably not native to the USA (Ward 2012: 476; Grewell et al. 2016). It was naturalized in Florida by 1966 (D'Arcy 990, FLAS).
This species contains oleandrin, a toxic cardiac glycoside (Palmisano et al. 2015) also investigated in medical research and for therapeutic potential (e.g. Ko et al. 2018).

This treatment may include plants referred to as N. pubescens, N. rubra, or hybrids thereof. Plants with crimson-red petals have been referred to as N. rubra, possibly a hybrid of N. lotus and N. pubescens. It is unclear how N. lotus (African) and N. pubescens (Asian) can be unequivocally distinguished; possibly N. pubescens has pinker petals more often (Hooker 1875; Wiersema 1982; Verdcourt 1989; Sharma et al. 1993; La-ongsri et al. 2009; Dkhar et al. 2010, 2013; Guruge et al. 2016).

Native to the Bahamas and Cuba (Acevedo-Rodríguez & Strong 2012), this species has a yellow corolla and is very similar to the white-flowered paleotropical species N. indica (Tippery et al. 2015). Because of its recent detection in Florida and the possibility of its cultivation (perhaps under a different name), N. grayana is tentatively considered non-native. The species may have also arrived in Florida as a natural range expansion (Tippery et al. 2015).

Common Name: MICKEY MOUSE PLANT; BIRD'S EYE BUSH

Plant Notes: This genus is native to Africa, the Seychelles, Madagascar, and Mascarene Islands (Garay & Taylor 1976). This species is considered non-native to the Neotropics, though its type specimen is from Brazil. It was first noticed in Florida in Miami-Dade County in 1974 (Austin 1978) and was vouchered from that spot, Luer & Hammer 1099 (FTG, SEL). This species is apparently commonly mycorrhizal with saprophytic species of Psathyrella (Bayman et al. 2016), suggesting the orchid is parasitizing the fungus. It has been proposed to transfer this species to the genus Eulophia (Chase et al. 2021).

According to de Oliveira & Montenegro Valls (2008), this species should take the earlier name P. lepton. The specific epithet was originally published as P. leptos but the spelling often has been changed to P. lepton. This species may also be able to hybridize with P. plicatulum (Costa Huber 2015).
In the proposed revision of Phyllanthus, this species has been moved to the genus Moeroris (Bouman et al. 2022).
In the proposed revision of Phyllanthus, this species has been moved to the genus Emblica (Bouman et al. 2022).

Its presence in Florida was originally conceived to be a rare endemic described as P. nebulosa (Lakela 1962, 1963). The lack of a clear morphological distinction and its disjunction in disturbed sites in Florida suggest it is an introduction of the widespread P. corymbosa.

Common Name: KARUM TREE; POONGA-OIL TREE; PONGAME OILTREE

Plant Notes: This species has a pappus of plumose bristles. The plant is otherwise superficially similar to Ageratum, which has a pappus of scales or a coronal rim.
Though originally published as "cattleianum", often the spelling is changed to "cattleyanum".
This species contains the deadly toxin ricin, a ribosome inactivating protein (Olnes 2004; Lapadula & Ayub 2017).
Ezcurra & Daniel (2007) established Ruellia simplex as the correct name for this species.

This cereal is sometimes infected with the ascomycete Claviceps purpurea, producing blackish sclerotia whose consumption has led to ergotism. Research on this fungus led to the use of ergotamine for hemorrhage and migraines and the synthesis of LSD.
The genus Cypselea has been subsumed into Sesuvium (Bohley et al. 2017)
This species falls outside Cleome s.str. and is now placed in Sieruela (Iltis & Cochrane 2007; Cochrane & Iltis 2014; Patchell et al. 2014; Roalson et al. 2015; Roalson & Hall 2017).

The earliest known collection in the USA may be the type specimen from 1852. This species is closely related to, and, perhaps, is conspecific with S. micranthum, which would be the earlier adopted name if considered synonymous (Tacuatiá et al. 2016; Shin et al. 2016). It seems possible that what is known as S. rosulatum in the USA is an early introduction of S. micranthum.
For an identification key to common species in Solanum sect. Lycopersicon, see Darwin et al. (2003).

Sporobolus jacquemontii is considered the accepted name, while S. indicus var. pyramidalis is apparently a misapplied name in Florida and is rather a taxon found in the Old World (Peterson et al. 2014; Overholt & Franck 2017). FNA (vol. 25) consider both S. indicus and S. jacquemontii as native to North America.

Native to Africa and Asia, this species was first detected in Polk Co. in 1978 (Shuey et al. 2156, USF),  primarily parasitizing Indigofera hirsuta as well as other Fabaceae (e.g. Alysicarpus, I. suffruticosa) in Florida (Musselman & Parker 1981).

Kirschner & Stepánek (2011) selected an uncited lectotype annotated by Linnaeus that is more congruent with the basionym protologue and current usage of T. officinale (T. sect. Taraxacum), as a previous incongruent lectotype selection is equated with the current sense of T. campylodes (T. sect. Crocea).
This species belongs in the genus Tripidium, which is distantly related to Saccharum (Welker et al. 2015; Vincent & Gardner 2016).

Based on morphology this species was moved to Urochloa by Webster (1987) which is supported by DNA studies (Salariato et al. 2010; Delfini et al. 2023; Masters et al. 2024). This species is often placed in the genus Megathyrsus (Simon & Jacobs 2003), which is relatively deeply nested in a broader Urochloa clade. Webster (1987: 242) wrote "The compound branching pattern of the primary branches is the only basis for placing this species in Panicum. It has numerous spikelet, vegetative and anatomical characteristics in common with other species of Urochloa (as defined here) and its transfer is taxonomically essential."
